_what: Movements the fundamentals list promises but the database did not hold. Added 2026-08-19 after Nicolas approved the structural fixes.

movements: Feet hip-width, soft knees. Push the hips back like closing a car door with them, chest stays proud. Feel the hamstrings lengthen, then drive the hips forward to stand. The knees barely move.
hips travel back not down; spine stays neutral throughout; shins near vertical at the bottom
Start in a hollow hold — low back pressed flat, arms and legs locked and lifted. Rock the whole body as one rigid unit from shoulders to hips. The shape never changes; only the contact point moves.
low back never leaves the floor; arms and legs stay locked; the rock comes from the whole body, not a hip pump

Half-kneeling, band or cable anchored at chest height to one side. Ribs down, glute of the down leg switched on. Rotate through the mid-back and pull the band across — the hips do not move. Return slowly.
hips stay square and still; rotation comes from the thoracic spine; no lean, no hip swivel
Wide stance. Sit down over one leg, keeping that heel flat, while the other leg straightens with the toes up. Chest tall. Push back up through the working heel and shift to the other side.
working heel stays down; hip crease reaches at least knee height; straight leg keeps its knee locked
Belt, vest or a dumbbell between the feet. Dead hang, chin clearly over the bar, controlled all the way down. Add load only once you own ten clean bodyweight reps.
dead-hang start; chin over the bar; no kip; the added load is stated with the rep count
Stand on one leg in front of a box or bench. Sit back and down under control until you touch, then stand without rocking. Lower the box as you get stronger — that is the whole progression.
controlled descent, no drop; touch not sit; stand up without the free leg or hands helping
Full depth on one leg, free leg held straight out in front, heel of the working leg flat on the floor. Ankle mobility usually fails before strength does — train it directly.
hamstring covers the calf at the bottom; free leg never touches down; no hand assist or momentum
Hold the free ankle behind you. Lower until the trailing knee touches the floor, torso upright, then stand. More knee-dominant than the pistol and kinder to the ankle.
trailing knee touches lightly; torso stays upright; no hand contact with the floor

Stand on a box with a LIGHT weight. Tuck the chin and roll down one vertebra at a time, letting the spine flex fully, then stack back up the same way. Load stays light for a long time — this is a mobility lift, not a strength lift.
segmental roll, not a hinge; legs stay straight; load light enough to control every vertebra
Lie on a bench and grip behind your head. Drive the whole body up so only the shoulders touch, then lower as ONE rigid plank — hips never bend. Stop the set the moment the hips break.
body stays one straight line from shoulders to toes; hips never pike; controlled 3-5 second lower
A burpee with the hard parts removed. Squat down, hands to the floor, walk or step the feet back to a plank, walk them in, stand up. No jump, no push-up. This is how a beginner earns the burpee.
hands reach the floor; hips reach full plank extension; stand fully upright at the top
A full burpee with FIVE push-ups at the bottom before you jump the feet in. The pumps are strict — chest to floor, full lockout, no worming.
five full-range push-ups per rep; chest touches each time; finish with a jump and full hip extension
Seven push-ups at the bottom of every burpee. This is a conditioning punishment, not a strength movement. Pace it or it paces you.
seven full-range push-ups per rep; no dropping to the knees; jump at the top
The skater jump. Push off one leg sideways, land on the other, absorb it and hold a beat before pushing back. Frontal-plane power, which almost nothing else in a programme trains.
land on one leg and stabilise before the next bound; knee tracks over the toes; distance not height
Drop into a reverse lunge, jump and switch legs in the air, land straight into the next lunge. Soft landings, chest tall.
back knee approaches the floor each rep; legs switch mid-air; landing is quiet
High anchor to low, or low to high. The arms stay long and the ROTATION comes from the torso, not the shoulders. Hips turn with you — this is real rotation, not a resisted twist.
torso rotates through a full arc; arms stay extended; movement is driven by the trunk not the arms
Half-kneeling kills the hips, so the rotation has to come from the mid-back. The cleanest way to learn what rotating actually feels like before you add speed or load.
down knee stays planted; hips face forward; rotation is thoracic
Load the back hip, then throw the ball into a wall by turning the hips and torso through. Full follow-through. This is rotational POWER — the output side of the pattern.
hips lead, torso follows, arms last; full follow-through; the ball leaves hard
Stand side-on to the anchor and press the handle straight out. The cable wants to twist you; your job is to refuse. Nothing moves except the arms.
hips and shoulders stay square throughout; no lean; arms lock out level with the sternum
